name: Washing Machine
blurb: On a cold wash, the machine itself uses only 0.3–0.5 kWh per load for the motor and controls. Hot washes are a different story: heating the water can multiply the true energy cost of a load by five or more, it just shows up on the water heater's tab.
tips: Wash cold by default — modern detergents are formulated for it, and water heating is most of a hot load's cost.
High spin speeds cost pennies and save dollars by cutting dryer time.
Full loads beat multiple small ones; the motor energy is nearly the same either way.

name: Electric Dryer
blurb: A conventional electric dryer is one of the most power-hungry appliances in the house, drawing around 5,000 watts and using 2.5–4 kWh per load. For a family drying five loads a week, it's frequently a top-three line item on the bill.
tips: Clean the lint filter every load and the vent duct yearly — restricted airflow directly extends every cycle.
Use the moisture sensor setting instead of timed dry; overdrying is pure waste.
Dry consecutive loads back-to-back to reuse residual heat.

name: Heat Pump Dryer
blurb: Heat pump dryers recycle their hot air instead of blowing it out a vent, using roughly 40–60% less electricity per load than conventional electric dryers. Cycles run longer, but the per-load cost drops to about a third.

name: Gas Dryer (Electric Components)
blurb: A gas dryer's heat comes from natural gas, but the drum motor and blower still use about 0.3–0.5 kWh of electricity per load. Its electric footprint is small — the gas meter carries the real cost.

name: Clothes Iron
blurb: Irons draw 1,000–1,800 watts but cycle their element once hot. A weekly half-hour ironing session lands around a third of a kilowatt-hour — noticeable wattage, negligible bill impact.

name: Garment Steamer
blurb: Handheld and upright steamers boil water at 1,000–1,800 watts for a few minutes per session. Touching up a few outfits a week costs less than a dollar a year in most states.
